Supply Chain Data - FMCG in Instant noodles¶

Business Context:¶

A fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) company that entered the instant noodles market two years ago is facing challenges in balancing demand and supply across its warehouses nationwide. In some regions, demand far exceeds supply, while in others, excess inventory is leading to wastage and higher costs. This mismatch results in significant inventory losses and missed sales opportunities. To remain competitive and profitable in the highly dynamic FMCG sector, the company needs a data-driven approach to optimize its supply chain and align production with regional demand patterns.

Objective:¶

As a data scientist, you are tasked with building a predictive model using historical sales and supply data to determine the optimum quantity of product to ship to each warehouse. Additionally, analyzing demand patterns across different regions will help management design targeted advertisement campaigns. Solving this problem will enable the company to minimize inventory costs, reduce stockouts, and drive higher sales through better demand forecasting and efficient supply chain management

Data Dictionary:¶

The dataset contains information about the historical sales patterns. The detailed data dictionary is given below:

  • Ware_house_ID: Product warehouse ID

  • WH_Manager_ID: Employee ID of warehouse manager

  • Location_type: Location of the warehouse, like in a city or a village

  • WH_capacity_siz: Storage capacity size of the warehouse

  • zone: Zone of the warehouse

  • WH_regional_zone: Regional zone of the warehouse under each zone

  • num_refill_req_l3m: Number of times refilling has been done in the last 3 months

  • transport_issue_l1y: Any transport issue, like an accident or goods stolen, reported in the last year

  • Competitor_in_mkt: Number of instant noodles competitors in the market

  • retail_shop_num: Number of retail shops that sell the product under the warehouse area

  • wh_owner_type: Company owns the warehouse, or they have rented the warehouse

  • distributor_num: Number of distributors working between the warehouse and retail shops

  • flood_impacted: Warehouse is in the flood-impacted area indicator

  • flood_proof: Warehouse is flood-proof. Like storage is at some height, not directly on the ground

  • electric_supply: The Warehouse has an electric backup, like a generator, so they can run the warehouse in load shedding

  • dist_from_hub: Distance between the warehouse to the production hub in Kms

  • workers_num: Number of workers working in the warehouse

  • wh_est_year: Warehouse established year

  • storage_issue_reported_l3m: Warehouse reported a storage issue to the corporate office in the last 3 months. Like rats, fungus due to moisture, etc.

  • temp_reg_mach: Warehouse has a temperature regulating machine indicator

  • approved_wh_govt_certificate: What kind of standard certificate has been issued to the warehouse from the government regulatory body

  • wh_breakdown_l3m: Number of times the warehouse faced a breakdown in the last 3 months. Like a strike by workers, a flood, or an electrical failure

  • govt_check_l3m: Number of times government officers have visited the warehouse to check the quality and expiry of stored food in the last 3 months

  • product_wg_ton: Product has been shipped in the last 3 months. Weight is in tons

Treating Missing values in the Data¶

In [ ]:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.impute import KNNImputer
from scipy.stats import pearsonr

# Step 1: Convert float years to integers
data['wh_est_year'] = data['wh_est_year'].astype('float')

# Step 2: Select features relevant for imputation
features_for_imputation = ['wh_est_year', 'workers_num', 'dist_from_hub', 'retail_shop_num']

# Step 3: Apply KNN imputer
imputer = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5)
data[features_for_imputation] = imputer.fit_transform(data[features_for_imputation])

# Step 4: Create warehouse_age
current_year = 2026
data['warehouse_age'] = current_year - data['wh_est_year'].round().astype(int)

# Step 5: Test significance of warehouse_age against product weight
subset = data[['warehouse_age', 'product_wg_ton']].dropna()
corr, pval = pearsonr(subset['warehouse_age'], subset['product_wg_ton'])
print("Correlation:", corr, "P-value:", pval)

# Step 6: Drop original wh_est_year if not needed
data = data.drop('wh_est_year', axis=1)

# Step 7: Check for remaining missing values
display(data.isnull().sum())

  • Lets us also check for their significance with target variable by ANOVA test. - ANOVA tests whether the mean product weight differs significantly across categories (e.g., flood-proof vs not flood-proof warehouses)

ANOVA Test of Significance between categorical variables and Target variable:¶

In [ ]:
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# wh_owner_type vs product weight
model_wo = smf.ols('product_wg_ton ~ C(wh_owner_type)', data=data).fit()
anova_wo = sm.stats.anova_lm(model_wo, typ=2)
print("\nwh_owner_type ANOVA:\n", anova_wo)

# WH_regional_zone vs product weight
model_Zo = smf.ols('product_wg_ton ~ C(WH_regional_zone)', data=data).fit()
anova_Zo = sm.stats.anova_lm(model_Zo, typ=2)
print("\nWH_regional_zone ANOVA:\n", anova_Zo)

# WH_capacity_size vs product weight
model_Ws = smf.ols('product_wg_ton ~ C(WH_capacity_size)', data=data).fit()
anova_Ws = sm.stats.anova_lm(model_Ws, typ=2)
print("\nWH_capacity_size ANOVA:\n", anova_Ws)

# Flood proof vs product weight
model_fp = smf.ols('product_wg_ton ~ C(flood_proof)', data=data).fit()
anova_fp = sm.stats.anova_lm(model_fp, typ=2)
print("\nFlood Proof ANOVA:\n", anova_fp)

# Flood impacted vs product weight
model_fi = smf.ols('product_wg_ton ~ C(flood_impacted)', data=data).fit()
anova_fi = sm.stats.anova_lm(model_fi, typ=2)
print("\nFlood Impacted ANOVA:\n", anova_fi)

# Electricity supply vs product weight
model_es = smf.ols('product_wg_ton ~ C(electric_supply)', data=data).fit()
anova_es = sm.stats.anova_lm(model_es, typ=2)
print("\nElectric Supply ANOVA:\n", anova_es)

Univariate and Bivariate analysis for Numeric Variables¶

In [ ]:
def plot_numerical_vs_target(data, col, target='product_wg_ton'):
    plt.figure(figsize=(8,4))
    ax = sns.scatterplot(data=data, x=col, y=target, alpha=0.6)
    sns.regplot(data=data, x=col, y=target, scatter=False, color='red')  # regression line
    plt.title(f"{target} vs {col}")
    plt.show()

numerical_cols = [
    'num_refill_req_l3m','transport_issue_l1y',
    'Competitor_in_mkt','retail_shop_num','distributor_num',
    'dist_from_hub','workers_num','warehouse_age',
    'storage_issue_reported_l3m','wh_breakdown_l3m',
    'govt_check_l3m','product_wg_ton'
]

for col in numerical_cols:
    plot_numerical_vs_target(data, col)
  • Num refill re l3m, competitor in market, retail shop num, distributor num, dist from hub, workers num, govt check l3m – these variables show no relationship with product weight as the graphs doesnot show any linear trend.
  • Transport issue l1y – downtrend or an inverse relationship – warehouses with more transport issues tend to handle lighter products. This may be due to an anticipation that heavy products need better transport.
  • Warehouse age, storage issue reported l3m, wh breakdown l3m – these variables show significant linear trend with product weight and are the useful predictors for product weight.
  • Strongest predictors: storage_issue_reported_l3m and warehouse_age show the most pronounced positive correlation with product_wg_ton.
  • Operational stress indicators: Features like wh_breakdown_l3m and num_refill_req_l3m may indirectly signal higher product volumes.
  • Weak or neutral predictors: transport_issue_l1y and Competitor_in_mkt show little to no relationship with the target.

Outlier treatment:¶

  • Outliers are seen in Location_type and approved_wh_govt_certificate variables.
  • They can be treated through IQR method or log transformation method.
  • However these are the real data that cannot be treated as they significantly impact the model. Hence we let them be and dont treat them.

Encoding Categorical Variables by Onehot encoding¶

  • Each category in a categorical feature is transformed into a new binary column.
  • The column takes the value 1 if the observation belongs to that category, otherwise 0.
  • This avoids assigning arbitrary numeric values (like 1, 2, 3) that could mislead models into thinking categories have an order.
In [ ]:
# Encoding
data = pd.get_dummies(data, drop_first=True)

Model Building:¶

Target Variable¶

product_wg_ton - Quantity shipped in last 3 months

Modeling Goal¶

Predict optimal shipment quantity per warehouse given:

  • Infrastructure
  • Market competition
  • Logistics risks

  • Regional characteristics

  • Since the regression is used when the target variable is continuos numeric data, we finally identify this as: # This is a supervised regression problem.

Defining X and Y(Target)¶

In [ ]:
# Define numeric and categorical column lists
numeric_cols = ['transport_issue_l1y','storage_issue_reported_l3m',
                'temp_reg_mach','wh_breakdown_l3m',
                'warehouse_age']   # exclude target here

categorical_cols = ['Location_type_Urban',
                    'WH_regional_zone_Zone 2','WH_regional_zone_Zone 3',
                    'WH_regional_zone_Zone 4','WH_regional_zone_Zone 5',
                    'WH_regional_zone_Zone 6',
                    'approved_wh_govt_certificate_A+',
                    'approved_wh_govt_certificate_Applied_Not_Received',
                    'approved_wh_govt_certificate_B',
                    'approved_wh_govt_certificate_B+',
                    'approved_wh_govt_certificate_C']

# Combine predictors
X = data[numeric_cols + categorical_cols]

# Target
y = data['product_wg_ton']

We choose 5 models for model building to check the performance of data.

  1. Linear regression model
  2. Decision tree model
  3. Random forest model
  4. Bagging model
  5. XG Boost model

1. Baseline Model – Linear Regression¶

Linear Regression was chosen as a baseline due to its simplicity, interpretability, and effectiveness as a reference point for more complex models

We are predicting the demand through a simple linear regression model initially¶

In [ ]:
import statsmodels.api as sm

# Step 1: Convert boolean columns to int (needed for statsmodels)
bool_cols = X_train.select_dtypes(include='bool').columns
X_train[bool_cols] = X_train[bool_cols].astype(int)
X_test[bool_cols] = X_test[bool_cols].astype(int)

# Step 2: Add constant (intercept)
X_train_sm = sm.add_constant(X_train)
X_test_sm = sm.add_constant(X_test)

# Step 3: Fit the model
olsmodel = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_sm).fit()

# Step 4: Print model summary
print(olsmodel.summary())

Calculating both Train and Test MAE and RMSE¶

  • This gives us a complete picture of model fit and generalization.
In [ ]:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
import numpy as np

# Predictions
y_train_pred = olsmodel.predict(X_train_sm)
y_test_pred  = olsmodel.predict(X_test_sm)

# Train MAE, RMSE, MAPE, R2
mae_train = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_train_pred)
rmse_train = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, y_train_pred))
mape_train = np.mean(np.abs((y_train - y_train_pred) / y_train)) * 100
r2_train = r2_score(y_train, y_train_pred)

# Adjusted R² for train
n_train = X_train_sm.shape[0]   # number of observations
p = X_train_sm.shape[1]         # number of predictors
adj_r2_train = 1 - (1 - r2_train) * (n_train - 1) / (n_train - p - 1)

# Test MAE, RMSE, MAPE, R2
mae_test = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_test_pred)
rmse_test = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_test_pred))
mape_test = np.mean(np.abs((y_test - y_test_pred) / y_test)) * 100
r2_test = r2_score(y_test, y_test_pred)

# Adjusted R² for test
n_test = X_test_sm.shape[0]
adj_r2_test = 1 - (1 - r2_test) * (n_test - 1) / (n_test - p - 1)

# Print results
print("Linear regression Train MAE:", mae_train)
print("Linear regression Train RMSE:", rmse_train)
print("Linear regression Train MAPE (%):", mape_train)
print("Linear regression Train R²:", r2_train)
print("Linear regression Train Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_train)

print("Linear regression Test MAE:", mae_test)
print("Linear regression Test RMSE:", rmse_test)
print("Linear regression Test MAPE (%):", mape_test)
print("Linear regression Test R²:", r2_test)
print("Linear regression Test Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_test)

  • Train MAPE = 6.16% / Test MAPE = 6.06% - Predictions are, on average, within ~6% of actual product weights. This is excellent accuracy for forecasting.

3. Building Random forest model¶

In [ ]:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
import numpy as np

# Initialize Random Forest model
rf_model = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=100,       # number of trees
    random_state=42,        # reproducibility
    max_depth=None,         # let trees grow fully (can tune later)
    n_jobs=-1               # use all cores for speed
)

# Fit the model
rf_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Predictions
y_train_pred_rf = rf_model.predict(X_train)
y_test_pred_rf = rf_model.predict(X_test)

# Train metrics
mae_train_rf = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_train_pred_rf)
rmse_train_rf = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, y_train_pred_rf))
mape_train_rf = np.mean(np.abs((y_train - y_train_pred_rf) / y_train)) * 100
r2_train_rf = r2_score(y_train, y_train_pred_rf)

# Adjusted R² for train
n_train = X_train.shape[0]   # number of observations
p = X_train.shape[1]         # number of predictors
adj_r2_train_rf = 1 - (1 - r2_train_rf) * (n_train - 1) / (n_train - p - 1)

# Test metrics
mae_test_rf = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_test_pred_rf)
rmse_test_rf = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_test_pred_rf))
mape_test_rf = np.mean(np.abs((y_test - y_test_pred_rf) / y_test)) * 100
r2_test_rf = r2_score(y_test, y_test_pred_rf)

# Adjusted R² for test
n_test = X_test.shape[0]
adj_r2_test_rf = 1 - (1 - r2_test_rf) * (n_test - 1) / (n_test - p - 1)

# Print results
print("Random Forest Train MAE:", mae_train_rf)
print("Random Forest Train RMSE:", rmse_train_rf)

print("Random Forest Test MAPE (%):", mape_test_rf)
print("Random Forest Test R²:", r2_test_rf)

4. Building Bagging model¶

In [ ]:
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
import numpy as np

# Initialize Bagging model with Decision Trees as base learners
bagging_model = BaggingRegressor(
    estimator=DecisionTreeRegressor(),
    n_estimators=100,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Fit the model
bagging_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Predictions
y_train_pred_bag = bagging_model.predict(X_train)
y_test_pred_bag = bagging_model.predict(X_test)

# Train metrics
mae_train_bag = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_train_pred_bag)
rmse_train_bag = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, y_train_pred_bag))
mape_train_bag = np.mean(np.abs((y_train - y_train_pred_bag) / y_train)) * 100
r2_train_bag = r2_score(y_train, y_train_pred_bag)

# Adjusted R² for train
n_train = X_train.shape[0]   # number of observations
p = X_train.shape[1]         # number of predictors
adj_r2_train_bag = 1 - (1 - r2_train_bag) * (n_train - 1) / (n_train - p - 1)

# Test metrics
mae_test_bag = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_test_pred_bag)
rmse_test_bag = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_test_pred_bag))
mape_test_bag = np.mean(np.abs((y_test - y_test_pred_bag) / y_test)) * 100
r2_test_bag = r2_score(y_test, y_test_pred_bag)

# Adjusted R² for test
n_test = X_test.shape[0]
adj_r2_test_bag = 1 - (1 - r2_test_bag) * (n_test - 1) / (n_test - p - 1)

# Print results
print("Bagging Train MAE:", mae_train_bag)
print("Bagging Train RMSE:", rmse_train_bag)
print("Bagging Train MAPE (%):", mape_train_bag)
print("Bagging Train R²:", r2_train_bag)
print("Bagging Train Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_train_bag)

print("Bagging Test MAE:", mae_test_bag)
print("Bagging Test RMSE:", rmse_test_bag)
print("Bagging Test MAPE (%):", mape_test_bag)
print("Bagging Test R²:", r2_test_bag)
print("Bagging Test Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_test_bag)

Bagging Train RMSE: 513.078910421441
Bagging Train MAPE (%): 2.060314938183841
Bagging Train R²: 0.9980586623369018
Bagging Train Adjusted R²: 0.9980568856737084
Bagging Test MAE: 677.0502954732042
Bagging Test RMSE: 918.3387195035842
Bagging Test MAPE (%): 4.155758348717517
Bagging Test R²: 0.9936449340548178

  • MAE: Training error is very low (~ 298 tons), while test error rises (~ 677 tons), showing some generalization gap but still acceptable.
  • RMSE: Training deviations are small (~ 513), test deviations larger (~918), indicating higher variance on unseen data.
  • MAPE: Training predictions deviate by ~2%, test predictions by ~4%, reflecting strong but slightly reduced accuracy on new data.
  • R²: Training fit is near perfect (0.998), test fit remains excellent (0.994), confirming the model explains almost all variance.
  • Adjusted R²: Training adjusted R² (0.99806) and test adjusted R² (0.99363) closely mirror R², validating that predictors are genuinely useful without overinflation

Bagging strikes a balance: it captures nonlinear relationships better than Linear Regression, avoids the extreme overfitting of a single Decision Tree, and performs comparably to Random Forest.

5. Building XG Boost model¶

In [ ]:
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
import numpy as np

# Initialize XGBoost model
xgb_model = XGBRegressor(
    n_estimators=200,
    learning_rate=0.1,
    max_depth=6,
    subsample=0.8,
    colsample_bytree=0.8,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Fit the model
xgb_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Predictions
y_train_pred_xgb = xgb_model.predict(X_train)
y_test_pred_xgb = xgb_model.predict(X_test)

# Train metrics
mae_train_xgb = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_train_pred_xgb)
rmse_train_xgb = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, y_train_pred_xgb))
mape_train_xgb = np.mean(np.abs((y_train - y_train_pred_xgb) / y_train)) * 100
r2_train_xgb = r2_score(y_train, y_train_pred_xgb)

# Adjusted R² for train
n_train = X_train.shape[0]   # number of observations
p = X_train.shape[1]         # number of predictors
adj_r2_train_xgb = 1 - (1 - r2_train_xgb) * (n_train - 1) / (n_train - p - 1)

# Test metrics
mae_test_xgb = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_test_pred_xgb)
rmse_test_xgb = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_test_pred_xgb))
mape_test_xgb = np.mean(np.abs((y_test - y_test_pred_xgb) / y_test)) * 100
r2_test_xgb = r2_score(y_test, y_test_pred_xgb)

# Adjusted R² for test
n_test = X_test.shape[0]
adj_r2_test_xgb = 1 - (1 - r2_test_xgb) * (n_test - 1) / (n_test - p - 1)

# Print results
print("XGBoost Train MAE:", mae_train_xgb)
print("XGBoost Train RMSE:", rmse_train_xgb)
print("XGBoost Train MAPE (%):", mape_train_xgb)
print("XGBoost Train R²:", r2_train_xgb)
print("XGBoost Train Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_train_xgb)

print("XGBoost Test MAE:", mae_test_xgb)
print("XGBoost Test RMSE:", rmse_test_xgb)
print("XGBoost Test MAPE (%):", mape_test_xgb)
print("XGBoost Test R²:", r2_test_xgb)
print("XGBoost Test Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_test_xgb)

Hyperparameter tuning¶

Typical Hyperparameters to Tune in the models - XGBOOST, Random forest, Bagging.

  • max_depth (limit tree depth)
  • min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf (control branching)
  • n_estimators (number of trees)
  • One can use GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV from scikit-learn

Hyperparameter tuning for Random forest model¶

In [204]:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

# Define parameter grid
param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [100, 200, 300],
    'max_depth': [None, 10, 20],
    'min_samples_split': [2, 5],
    'min_samples_leaf': [1, 2],
    'max_features': ['sqrt'] # Changed 'auto' to 'sqrt'
}

# Initialize model
rf_model = RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)

# Grid search
grid_search_rf = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=rf_model,
    param_grid=param_grid,
    cv=3,
    scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error',
    n_jobs=-1
)

grid_search_rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("Best parameters:", grid_search_rf.best_params_)
print("Best score:", -grid_search_rf.best_score_)

Best parameters: {'max_depth': None, 'max_features': 'sqrt', 'min_samples_leaf': 1, 'min_samples_split': 2, 'n_estimators': 200}
Best score: 913.4734803446709

Hyperparameter tuning for Bagging model¶

In [202]:
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

# Define parameter grid
param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [50, 100, 200],
    'max_samples': [0.5, 0.7, 1.0],
    'max_features': [0.5, 0.7, 1.0],
    'bootstrap': [True, False]
}

# Initialize model (using DecisionTreeRegressor as base estimator)
bag_model = BaggingRegressor(
    estimator=DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42),
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Grid search
grid_search_bag = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=bag_model,
    param_grid=param_grid,
    cv=3,
    scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error',
    n_jobs=-1
)

grid_search_bag.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("Best parameters:", grid_search_bag.best_params_)
print("Best score:", -grid_search_bag.best_score_)

Retraining tuned XG boost on full training set¶

In [206]:
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
import numpy as np

# Retrain tuned XGBoost with best parameters
xgb_tuned = XGBRegressor(
    colsample_bytree=1.0,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_depth=6,
    n_estimators=200,
    subsample=0.8,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Fit on full training set
xgb_tuned.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Predictions
y_train_pred_xgb_tuned = xgb_tuned.predict(X_train)
y_test_pred_xgb_tuned = xgb_tuned.predict(X_test)

# Helper function for Adjusted R²
def adjusted_r2(r2, n, p):
    return 1 - (1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - p - 1)

# Train metrics
mae_train_xgb_tuned = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_train_pred_xgb_tuned)
rmse_train_xgb_tuned = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, y_train_pred_xgb_tuned))
mape_train_xgb_tuned = np.mean(np.abs((y_train - y_train_pred_xgb_tuned) / y_train)) * 100
r2_train_xgb_tuned = r2_score(y_train, y_train_pred_xgb_tuned)
adj_r2_train_xgb_tuned = adjusted_r2(r2_train_xgb_tuned, X_train.shape[0], X_train.shape[1])

# Test metrics
mae_test_xgb_tuned = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_test_pred_xgb_tuned)
rmse_test_xgb_tuned = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_test_pred_xgb_tuned))
mape_test_xgb_tuned = np.mean(np.abs((y_test - y_test_pred_xgb_tuned) / y_test)) * 100
r2_test_xgb_tuned = r2_score(y_test, y_test_pred_xgb_tuned)
adj_r2_test_xgb_tuned = adjusted_r2(r2_test_xgb_tuned, X_test.shape[0], X_test.shape[1])

# Print results
print("Tuned XGBoost Train MAE:", mae_train_xgb_tuned)
print("Tuned XGBoost Train RMSE:", rmse_train_xgb_tuned)
print("Tuned XGBoost Train MAPE (%):", mape_train_xgb_tuned)
print("Tuned XGBoost Train R²:", r2_train_xgb_tuned)
print("Tuned XGBoost Train Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_train_xgb_tuned)

print("Tuned XGBoost Test MAE:", mae_test_xgb_tuned)
print("Tuned XGBoost Test RMSE:", rmse_test_xgb_tuned)
print("Tuned XGBoost Test MAPE (%):", mape_test_xgb_tuned)
print("Tuned XGBoost Test R²:", r2_test_xgb_tuned)
print("Tuned XGBoost Test Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_test_xgb_tuned)

mae_test_bag_tuned = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_test_pred_bag_tuned)
rmse_test_bag_tuned = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_test_pred_bag_tuned))
mape_test_bag_tuned = np.mean(np.abs((y_test - y_test_pred_bag_tuned) / y_test)) * 100
r2_test_bag_tuned = r2_score(y_test, y_test_pred_bag_tuned)
adj_r2_test_bag_tuned = adjusted_r2(r2_test_bag_tuned, X_test.shape[0], X_test.shape[1])

# Print results
print("Tuned Bagging Train MAE:", mae_train_bag_tuned)
print("Tuned Bagging Train RMSE:", rmse_train_bag_tuned)
print("Tuned Bagging Train MAPE (%):", mape_train_bag_tuned)
print("Tuned Bagging Train R²:", r2_train_bag_tuned)
print("Tuned Bagging Train Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_train_bag_tuned)

print("Tuned Bagging Test MAE:", mae_test_bag_tuned)
print("Tuned Bagging Test RMSE:", rmse_test_bag_tuned)
print("Tuned Bagging Test MAPE (%):", mape_test_bag_tuned)
print("Tuned Bagging Test R²:", r2_test_bag_tuned)
print("Tuned Bagging Test Adjusted R²:", adj_r2_test_bag_tuned)

Vizualizing the feature importances:¶

In [213]:
feature_names = X_train.columns
importances = xgb_tuned.feature_importances_
indices = np.argsort(importances)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 12))
plt.title("Feature Importances")
plt.barh(range(len(indices)), importances[indices], color="violet", align="center")
plt.yticks(range(len(indices)), [feature_names[i] for i in indices])
plt.xlabel("Relative Importance")
plt.show()
  • Our model is highly reliant on one feature, which can be both a strength and a risk:
  • If that feature is stable and well-measured, it drives excellent performance.
  • If it’s noisy, missing, or changes over time, the model may degrade quickly

The tight clustering of points around the diagonal line indicates:

  • Strong correlation between predicted and actual values
  • High predictive accuracy
  • Minimal bias or error
  • No major outliers suggests the model generalizes well

The model is reliable and well-calibrated, making it suitable for deployment or business reporting.

Executive Summary¶

We tested three advanced machine learning models — XGBoost, Random Forest, and Bagging — to predict warehouse performance using historical data. After tuning each model for accuracy and reliability, XGBoost emerged as the best performer.

  • It consistently gave the most accurate predictions on unseen data.
  • It explained over 99% of the variation in warehouse outcomes.
  • It had the lowest error rates, meaning its predictions are close to reality. The model relies heavily on one key factor: whether storage issues were reported in the last 3 months. This single feature drives most of the predictive power.

Business Recommendations¶

Prioritize Storage Issue Tracking, since recent storage issues are the strongest predictor of warehouse performance, ensure this data is captured accurately and consistently.

  • Consider automating alerts or dashboards around this metric.
  • Use the XGBoost Model for Forecasting
  • Deploy the tuned XGBoost model to predict warehouse risk or performance.
  • Integrate it into our reporting tools to support proactive decision-making.
  • Simplify Data Collection as many other features (certifications, zones, equipment) had minimal impact.
  • Focus data efforts on the few variables that truly matter — this reduces complexity and improves efficiency.
  • Monitor Model Stability because the model depends heavily on one feature, keep an eye on its quality and consistency.
  • Revalidate the model periodically to ensure it continues to perform well.
  • Communicate Insights Clearly and share the model’s findings with warehouse managers and operations teams.
  • Use simple visuals (like the observed vs predicted plot) to build trust and understanding.

This approach helps us move from reactive response to predictive, data-driven warehouse management — saving time, reducing risk, and improving service.
